corpus_definition: unable to stop doing something because you need it very much
usage_note: be / become / get addicted to + noun or -ing: 'He is addicted to coffee.' 'She got addicted to playing online games.' The 'to' is a preposition, so use -ing after it, not the infinitive.

relations.note: Very close, informal: 'He's hooked on video games.'
More formal; often about drugs, medicine or alcohol, or needing a person for help.
Related: you think about something all the time, but you don't need it in your body.
Related, informal and positive: you like something very much.

context.text: My younger brother is addicted to his phone. He says he can stop any time, but he has been addicted to social media since he was twelve.

reviewer_note: kind_hint was phrasal; corrected to phrase (adjective + preposition, not verb + particle). Note on 'to + -ing' trap.

corpus_definition: A feeling of deep respect and liking.

forms.definition: a feeling of great respect and liking for someone or something
forms.example: I have great admiration for doctors who work at night.

syn.note: Close; respect is about thinking someone is good, admiration adds liking and wonder.
Formal word for a good opinion of someone.
Related: you think something is good or right, but the feeling is weaker.
Related: praise is what you say; admiration is what you feel.

ant.note: A feeling that someone is worthless and not worth respect.
A strong feeling that someone or something is stupid or not good enough.

forms.definition: to respect and like someone or something very much
forms.example: Many young people admire their grandparents.

syn.note: Close, but without the feeling of liking or wonder.
Easy phrasal verb, used about people you want to be like.
Related: you see that something is good and are thankful for it.
Related: you say good things about someone; you can admire someone silently.

ant.note: To feel that someone is very bad and has no value.
To think you are better than someone.

forms.definition: very good and deserving respect
forms.example: Her patience with the children is admirable.

syn.note: Close and more common in everyday English.
Formal: deserving to be praised.
Related: very good, but about quality, not about respect.

ant.note: So bad that people should feel ashamed.

forms.definition: showing that you respect and like someone very much
forms.example: She gave her teacher an admiring look.

forms.definition: in a way that shows great respect and liking
forms.example: The children looked admiringly at the famous footballer.

syn.note: Related: in a way that shows you think something is good.

ant.note: In a way that shows you think someone is stupid or worthless.

forms.definition: very well, in a way that deserves respect
forms.example: The young team played admirably in the final.

people.definition: a person who likes and respects someone or something very much
people.example: The singer has many admirers in Uzbekistan.

context.text: My little sister is full of admiration for her teacher. She admires how patient the teacher is, and she always talks admiringly about her lessons.

reviewer_note: Admiral (navy officer) looks similar but is not family. Admirable is formal and means 'deserving admiration', not 'feeling it'.

corpus_definition: To respect someone for something good they have done.
usage_note: admire + person + for + noun / -ing: 'I admire her for her hard work.' 'We admire him for staying calm.' You can also say 'admire someone's + noun': 'I admire her courage.'

relations.note: Same pattern: 'respect someone for something'. Respect has less liking in it.
Easy phrasal verb, about a person you want to be like; no 'for' after it.
Related: 'praise someone for something' means you say it out loud.
Related: you see the value of what someone did and feel thankful.
To feel that someone is very bad: 'despise someone for lying'.
To say someone did something wrong: 'blame someone for something'.

context.text: Everyone in our village admires Aziza for her hard work. She runs a small bakery and still finds time to help her neighbours, and I admire her for that too.

reviewer_note: Pattern item; sb = somebody. Context shows the object between admire and for.

corpus_definition: to say that something is true, especially when you are unhappy.

forms.definition: a statement saying that something bad is true, often something you did wrong
forms.example: His admission of the mistake surprised everyone.
forms.note: Admission also means the right to enter a place or the price of a ticket: 'Admission is free.'

syn.note: Close; a confession is often about a crime or a sin.
Formal. American spelling: acknowledgment.

ant.note: A statement saying that something is not true.

forms.definition: permission to go into a place
forms.example: The sign on the door said 'No admittance'.
forms.note: Belongs to admit = let someone enter, not saying something is true. Formal.

forms.definition: to agree that something is true, often when you don't want to
forms.example: He had to admit that he was wrong.

syn.note: Close, but stronger: often about something very bad or secret.
Formal: to accept that something is true.
Informal phrasal verb: 'own up to a mistake'.
Related: 'accept that…' means you agree it is true, maybe without saying it.

ant.note: To say that something is not true.

forms.definition: having said openly that something, usually bad, is true about yourself
forms.example: He is an admitted fan of very loud music.

syn.note: Close; often 'self-confessed' in everyday English.

forms.definition: allowed, especially as evidence in a court of law
forms.example: The judge said the video was admissible as evidence.
forms.note: Belongs to admit = allow or accept, used in law; not saying something is true about yourself. Formal.

forms.definition: used to say that something is true, even if it weakens what you are saying
forms.example: Admittedly, I didn't study very hard for the test.

syn.note: Related: used the same way before 'but': 'Certainly it's expensive, but it's good.'

context.text: Bekzod finally admitted that he broke the window. His admission surprised his parents, but admittedly, he felt much better after telling the truth.

reviewer_note: Map keeps the 'say it is true' sense; admittance and admissible belong to 'let in / allow'. Admission has both senses, noted. No -sion affix claimed (admit -> admis- is not a clean split).

corpus_definition: A person who gives help and suggestions.

forms.definition: a person whose job is to help people make good decisions
forms.example: The financial adviser helped me save money.
forms.note: Also spelled advisor, especially in American English.

syn.note: An expert paid to give help, usually to a company.
Often helps with personal problems or study. American spelling: counselor.
Related: an older, experienced person who helps a younger one over a long time.
Related: someone who shows you the way, often on a trip.

forms.definition: an opinion someone gives you about what you should do
forms.example: My father gave me some good advice about money.
forms.note: Uncountable: 'some advice', 'a piece of advice', never 'an advice'. Noun advice has c; verb advise has s.

forms.definition: to tell someone what you think they should do
forms.example: The doctor advised me to drink more water.

syn.note: Close; recommend is often about a thing: 'recommend a hotel'.
Softer and more common in everyday English.
Formal; often used about personal problems.
Related, easy word: 'She told me to rest.'

forms.definition: having the job of giving help and suggestions, without making decisions
forms.example: She works for an advisory group at the ministry.

syn.note: Very formal word with the same meaning.

forms.definition: sensible and a good idea in a situation
forms.example: It is advisable to book train tickets early in summer.
forms.note: Formal. Opposite: inadvisable.

forms.definition: after thinking carefully, on purpose
forms.example: I use the word 'dangerous' advisedly.
forms.note: Belongs to advise = think carefully before acting, not giving help to others. Formal and not common.

context.text: My uncle works as a financial adviser in Tashkent. He advises families on how to save money, and his advice is always simple and clear.

reviewer_note: Person-noun headword stays main noun; advice (c) vs advise (s) spelling trap noted; adviser/advisor spelling noted.

corpus_definition: A warm, loving feeling for someone.

forms.definition: a feeling of liking and caring about someone
forms.example: He showed great affection for his pet dog.

syn.note: Very close; a gentle feeling of liking.
Easy word; love is usually stronger.
A friendly, kind feeling or way of acting.
A gentle, careful kind of love.
Related: worrying about someone and helping them.

ant.note: A feeling of not liking someone.
Unfriendly, angry feelings or behaviour towards someone.

forms.note: There is no verb for this meaning. Affect (to change or influence something) shares an old root but has a different meaning.

forms.definition: showing in a warm way that you love or like someone
forms.example: My grandmother is very affectionate with all her grandchildren.

syn.note: Very close and very common.
Friendly and kind.
Kind and helpful to others.
Gentle and loving.

forms.definition: in a warm way that shows love or liking
forms.example: She smiled affectionately at her baby son.

syn.note: Very close.
Close; also used about memories: 'remember fondly'.
In a friendly, kind way.

ant.note: In an unfriendly way, without feeling.

context.text: My grandmother in Bukhara is very affectionate. She hugs us every time we visit and speaks to us with great affection.

reviewer_note: Affect / affected (influence; not natural) kept out as not_family: same old root, unrelated meaning for learners. No -ion affix claimed.

corpus_definition: not too expensive for people to buy

forms.definition: how cheap or expensive something is for ordinary people
forms.example: The affordability of housing is a big problem in big cities.

syn.note: Related: cheapness can also mean low quality.

forms.definition: to have enough money to pay for something
forms.example: We can't afford a new car this year.
forms.note: Usually with can / could / be able to: 'I can't afford it.'

syn.note: Easy; 'can pay for' is close to 'can afford'.
Related: 'manage to buy' means you can do it, but with effort.
Related: to give money or time that you don't need yourself.

forms.definition: cheap enough for most people to pay for
forms.example: They offer affordable meals for students.

syn.note: Very close and a little formal.
Easy word, but cheap can also mean low quality.
Used about prices that are fair, not too high.

forms.note: There is no common adverb; affordably is very rare.

context.text: Students in Samarkand need affordable flats near the university. Many of them can't afford to live alone, so they share rooms with friends.

reviewer_note: Unaffordable placed in ant (negative prefix, rule 3). Affordably left as no_form (very rare).

corpus_definition: A business that provides a service for others.

forms.definition: a company that does work or arranges things for other people
forms.example: They hired a travel agency to plan their trips.
forms.note: Also a government office with a special job: 'a space agency'.

syn.note: A company, often one that gives a professional service.
Formal; an office that gives information or a service.
Related, easy word for any business.
Related: the place where the work is done.

forms.note: There is no verb made from agency.
There is no common adjective made from agency.
There is no adverb made from agency.

people.definition: a person whose job is to act or do business for other people
people.example: A travel agent booked our hotel in Istanbul.

context.text: My sister works at a travel agency in Tashkent. Every day, she and the other agents help families plan trips to Turkey and Dubai.

reviewer_note: Single-form family; agent shown in People & things. No -cy affix (not in the table).

corpus_definition: a situation where two or more people share the same opinion or decision

forms.definition: a situation where people have the same opinion or decide the same thing
forms.example: They finally reached an agreement about the plans.
forms.note: Also a written promise between people or countries: 'sign an agreement'.

syn.note: Formal: everyone in a group has the same opinion.
Formal, often in 'in accord with'.
Related: an informal agreement that is not written down.
Related, easy word: an agreement, often in business.

ant.note: A situation where people have different opinions.

forms.definition: to have the same opinion as someone else
forms.example: I agree with you about the new timetable.

syn.note: Very formal.
Related: you say yes to an idea, but maybe you don't share the opinion.

forms.definition: decided by everyone in a discussion
forms.example: We met at the agreed time outside the cinema.

syn.note: Decided and not going to change.
Related: used about times and prices that will not change.

forms.definition: pleasant and nice
forms.example: We spent an agreeable evening with our neighbours.
forms.note: Belongs to agree = be pleasant or suit someone (the weather agrees with me), not sharing an opinion. Formal; it can also mean 'willing to say yes'.

forms.definition: in a pleasant way
forms.example: We were agreeably surprised by the hotel.
forms.note: Goes with agreeable = pleasant, not with sharing an opinion.

context.text: After a long talk, my parents reached an agreement about our summer holiday. They both agreed to visit Khiva, and we leave on the agreed date, the first of July.

reviewer_note: Agreeable/agreeably are false friends (pleasant), shown as other_meaning. Disagreement / disagree in ant lists, not forms.

corpus_definition: Any vehicle that can fly through the air.

forms.definition: any machine that flies, such as a plane or helicopter
forms.example: The military aircraft flew over the city.
forms.note: The plural is the same: one aircraft, two aircraft (not 'aircrafts').

syn.note: Easy, everyday word, but only for planes with wings.
British English. American English: airplane.
Related: a fast plane with jet engines.
Related: one kind of aircraft, with blades on top.

forms.note: There is no verb made from aircraft.
There is no adjective made from aircraft.
There is no adverb made from aircraft.

context.text: Dozens of aircraft land at Tashkent airport every day. The newest aircraft are quieter and use less fuel than the old ones.

reviewer_note: Compound headword (air + craft); no forms. Plural trap noted: aircraft, not aircrafts.
